title: Probability Density Function
body:
For a discrete [[Random Variable]] you list the outcomes and their probabilities. For a continuous
one there are uncountably many outcomes, so that list cannot exist, and **the density is what
replaces it.**

## Why $P(X = x) = 0$

If every value in an interval had positive probability, uncountably many positive numbers would sum
past $1$. So each individual value gets probability exactly zero, and probability lives on
*intervals* instead:

$$
P(a \leq X \leq b) = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx
$$

Two consequences. **$f(x)$ is not a probability**: it is a probability *per unit of $x$*, it has
units, and it is allowed to exceed $1$ (a uniform on $[0, 0.1]$ has density $10$ everywhere on it).
And **$<$ versus $\leq$ stops mattering**, since the endpoints contribute zero area. That is a real
simplification, not a subtlety to worry about.

A valid density needs exactly two things:

$$
f(x) \geq 0 \quad\text{everywhere}, \qquad \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx = 1
$$

The normalisation is what fixes the constant in front. Given a shape you like, you integrate it and
divide by the answer, which is where $\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}$ in the [[Normal Distribution]]
comes from and why the exponential's $\lambda$ appears both in the exponent and in front.

**That second condition is usually an improper integral**, taken over an infinite domain, and it
converges because the tail decays fast enough. This is the point where [[CALCULUS 1]] stops being a
formality: a distribution is only legal if a limit at infinity exists. [[CALCULUS 2]]'s integration
techniques ([[Integration By Parts]] in particular) are what evaluate the exponential and gamma
cases by hand.

## The CDF

$$
F(x) = P(X \leq x) = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f(t)\,dt
$$

The CDF is the antiderivative of the density, so $f = F'$ by the fundamental theorem of calculus,
and

$$
P(a < X < b) = F(b) - F(a)
$$

**Every table lookup and every calculator function in this course is a CDF**, including the
$z$-table, and that is worth saying out loud because the tables are never labelled as such. $F$ is
non-decreasing, runs from $0$ to $1$, and exists for discrete variables too (as a step function),
which makes it the one description that works for both kinds.

Inverting it gives quantiles: $F^{-1}(0.5)$ is the [[Median]], $F^{-1}(0.975)$ is the critical value
a 95% [[Confidence Interval]] is built from. It is also how you generate samples from an arbitrary
distribution given only a uniform one, which is the standard trick behind [[Random Numbers]] and
[[Simulation]].

## The dictionary

| Discrete | Continuous |
|---|---|
| $p(x) = P(X = x)$ | $f(x)$, a density |
| $\sum_x p(x) = 1$ | $\int f(x)\,dx = 1$ |
| $E[X] = \sum x\,p(x)$ | $E[X] = \int x f(x)\,dx$ |
| $F(x) = \sum_{t \leq x} p(t)$ | $F(x) = \int_{-\infty}^x f(t)\,dt$ |

Sums become integrals and nothing else changes. Every theorem in block 2 has both forms and they
are proved the same way.

## Related

- [[Random Variable]]: the object this describes
- [[Probability Distribution]]: the specific continuous families
- [[Normal Distribution]]: the density whose CDF has no closed form, which is why the table exists
- [[Riemann Sum]] ([[CALCULUS 1]]): a discrete expectation $\sum x_i p_i$ *is* a Riemann sum of
  the continuous one, which is the precise sense in which the two cases are the same theory
- [[Improper Integral]] ([[CALCULUS 2]]): the normalisation $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f = 1$ is
  improper for every density on an unbounded domain, so a density is legal only because that limit
  converges. The Gaussian case is evaluated with a [[Double Integral]] in polar coordinates
- [[Integral]] ([[CALCULUS 1]]) and [[Integration Techniques]] ([[CALCULUS 2]]): the machinery
